items.name: Short-acting β2 agonists
items.how: β2 agonist → ↑ cAMP → bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation
hx: β2 antagonist → ↓ cAMP → bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation
It's an agonist; raised cAMP relaxes the muscle.
β1 agonist → ↑ cAMP → bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation
Airway relaxation is through β2; β1 drives the heart.
Mast-cell stabiliser → ↓ histamine → bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation
That's cromoglicate; salbutamol relaxes muscle directly through β2.
items.sewhy: Systemic β2 stimulation causes tremor in skeletal muscle, tachycardia (partly via β1), and drives potassium into cells (hypokalaemia); high doses raise lactate.

ci.why: Direct β stimulation of the heart
x: Vagal stimulation of the AV node
Vagal effects slow the heart; salbutamol stimulates β receptors.
Coronary vasoconstriction
It doesn't constrict coronaries; it stimulates cardiac β receptors.
QT shortening
Not the mechanism; direct β stimulation speeds the heart.
Increases urinary K⁺ loss
The fall is a shift into cells (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), not renal loss.
Blocks K⁺ absorption from the gut
No; it shifts K⁺ into cells.
Drives K⁺ out of cells
The opposite: it drives K⁺ in (which is why it treats hyperkalaemia).
Raises thyroxine production
It doesn't affect the thyroid; it adds to sympathetic effects.
Blocks carbimazole absorption
No interaction; it adds sympathetic stimulation.
Causes thyroid eye disease
No; it worsens tremor and tachycardia.

items.name: Long-acting β2 agonists
items.how: Long-acting β2 agonism (12 h); formoterol also works fast
hx: Long-acting β2 antagonism (12 h); salmeterol also works fast
LABAs are agonists, and formoterol is the fast one.
Long-acting β2 agonism (24 h); salmeterol also works fast
About 12 h, and salmeterol is slow; formoterol is fast.
Long-acting anti-inflammatory (12 h); formoterol also reduces eosinophils
LABAs relax smooth muscle; they don't treat inflammation (hence the ICS).
se: Same as SABAs: tremor, palpitations, hypokalaemia
items.sewhy: They act on the same receptors as SABAs for longer, so the effects are the same: tremor, palpitations and low potassium.

ci.why: LABA alone masks worsening inflammation → ↑ asthma deaths
x: LABA alone causes tachyphylaxis → no bronchodilation
The danger is masking inflammation, which raised deaths.
LABA alone thickens airway mucus → plugging
No; it masks worsening inflammation.
LABA alone triggers eosinophilia → ↑ exacerbations
LABAs don't cause eosinophilia; they hide worsening inflammation.

items.name: Inhaled corticosteroids
items.how: Anti-inflammatory gene effects in airway: ↓ cytokines and eosinophils
hx: Antihistamine effects in airway: block H1 receptors on smooth muscle
Not H1 block; they switch off inflammatory gene expression.
Anti-inflammatory gene effects in airway: ↑ cytokines and eosinophils
They reduce cytokines and eosinophils.
Leukotriene synthesis block in airway: inhibit 5-lipoxygenase
That's zileuton; ICS act through glucocorticoid receptors on genes.
se: Adrenal suppression, growth slowing, bone loss (high dose)
items.sewhy: Steroid deposited in the mouth and throat suppresses local immunity (thrush) and affects the vocal cords (hoarseness); absorbed steroid at high doses suppresses the adrenals, growth and bone, and in COPD it impairs lung defence (pneumonia).

x: Lowers TB drug levels
No interaction; local immune suppression is the concern.
Causes lung fibrosis
Not the concern; they suppress local immunity.
Masks a positive Mantoux test
Not the reason; they suppress local airway immunity.
ICS reduces antibiotic penetration
No; ICS themselves raise pneumonia risk.
ICS causes bronchiectasis
No; they raise pneumonia risk.
ICS masks fever in pneumonia
Not the concern; ICS increase pneumonia risk.

items.name: Inhaled antimuscarinics

uses.t: Asthma add-on and acute severe asthma

items.how: Block M3 receptors → ↓ bronchoconstriction and mucus
hx: Stimulate M3 receptors → ↓ bronchoconstriction and mucus
They block M3; acetylcholine normally constricts airways.
Block M2 receptors → ↑ acetylcholine release and mucus clearance
M2 block would raise ACh release; they target M3.
Block nicotinic receptors → ↓ bronchoconstriction and mucus
The receptors are muscarinic (M3).
items.sewhy: Some absorbed drug blocks muscarinic receptors elsewhere: salivary glands (dry mouth), bladder (retention), gut (constipation) and eyes (blurred vision).

ci.why: Pupil dilation blocks the drainage angle (nebuliser mist)
x: Pupil constriction blocks the drainage angle (nebuliser mist)
Antimuscarinics dilate the pupil; the iris crowds the angle.
Raised aqueous production floods the eye
Not production; the dilated iris blocks drainage.
Dry eyes scar the trabecular meshwork
No; pupil dilation closes the angle.
Constricts the prostate
No; it weakens detrusor contraction.
Increases urine production
Not diuresis; the detrusor contracts less.
Causes bladder spasm
The opposite: detrusor contraction weakens.

items.name: Montelukast
hx: Blocks leukotriene synthesis (5-lipoxygenase)
That's zileuton; montelukast blocks the CysLT1 receptor.
Blocks histamine (H1) receptors
It blocks leukotriene receptors.
Stimulates leukotriene (CysLT1) receptors
It's an antagonist.
items.sewhy: Blocking leukotriene receptors is generally well tolerated, but it can cause neuropsychiatric effects (nightmares, agitation, depression), which carry an MHRA warning.

ci.why: MHRA warning on mood and behaviour changes
x: MHRA warning on liver failure
The warning is neuropsychiatric (mood, sleep, behaviour).
Interacts with SSRIs
No interaction; montelukast itself can alter mood.
MHRA warning on weight gain and diabetes
The warning is about mood and behaviour.

items.name: Theophylline
hx: Phosphodiesterase activation and adenosine agonism
It inhibits PDE (↑ cAMP) and blocks adenosine.
Histamine (H1) antagonism and mast-cell stabilisation
Not an antihistamine; it inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition and respiratory stimulation
It inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine.
items.sewhy: Theophylline inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine, stimulating heart and brain; the safe range is narrow, so small level rises cause nausea, arrhythmias and seizures.

x: Raises the seizure threshold
It lowers it (adenosine is a natural anticonvulsant).
Speeds up antiepileptic metabolism
Not the issue; it lowers the seizure threshold.
Causes hyponatraemia
Not through sodium; it lowers the seizure threshold.
Bradycardic
It speeds the heart and is pro-arrhythmic.
Negatively inotropic
It's pro-arrhythmic (tachyarrhythmias).
QT-shortening
Not the issue; it's pro-arrhythmic.
Lower theophylline levels → loss of effect
They inhibit its metabolism, raising levels.
Raise antibiotic levels → ototoxicity
Theophylline levels rise, risking toxicity.
Block theophylline absorption → treatment failure
No absorption effect; levels rise.

items.name: Oxygen (controlled)
hx: Raises haemoglobin concentration
Oxygen doesn't make more haemoglobin; it raises FiO₂.
Stimulates the respiratory centre
It raises inspired oxygen, not respiratory drive.
Lowers alveolar CO₂ directly
It raises inspired O₂; CO₂ may rise in retainers.
items.sewhy: In CO₂ retainers, high oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch and reduces ventilatory drive, so CO₂ rises; dry gas irritates mucosa, and oxygen makes fires burn fiercely.

ci.why: High-flow O₂ worsens hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect
x: High-flow O₂ causes oxygen toxicity in the brain within minutes
The issue is CO₂ retention from V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect.
High-flow O₂ dries secretions, causing mucus plugging and hypoxia
Not mucus; it worsens hypercapnia.
High-flow O₂ lowers CO₂ too fast, causing alkalosis
CO₂ rises, not falls.
Oxygen toxicity
The danger is fire and burns.
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Not CO; oxygen feeds fires.
Worse CO₂ retention
The danger is burns and fires.

items.name: Varenicline
items.how: Partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors: reduces cravings and the reward from smoking
hx: Full agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors: replaces nicotine's reward completely
As a partial agonist it eases cravings and blunts the reward.
Antagonist at μ-opioid receptors: blocks the pleasure of smoking
That's naltrexone-like; varenicline is a nicotinic partial agonist.
Inhibits dopamine reuptake: reduces cravings and withdrawal
That's bupropion's action; varenicline works at α4β2 nicotinic receptors.
items.sewhy: Partial stimulation of nicotinic receptors in the gut and brain causes nausea and vivid dreams or sleep disturbance.

x: Proven teratogen; use bupropion
No proven harm, just no data; NRT is preferred (bupropion is avoided too).
Causes fetal nicotine addiction; use e-cigarettes
Not the reason; there's no safety data, so NRT is used.
Triggers preterm labour; stop smoking unaided
No; there's no safety data, so use NRT.
Monitor lithium levels
No lithium interaction; watch for mood change.
Monitor liver function
The concern is mood and behaviour.
Monitor blood glucose
Watch mood, not glucose.
Nephrotoxic
Not nephrotoxic; it accumulates.
Hepatically cleared
It's renally cleared, so reduce the dose.
Causes hyperkalaemia
Not the issue; it's renally cleared.

items.name: Nicotine replacement
items.how: Replaces nicotine without tar and carbon monoxide
hx: Blocks nicotine receptors so smoking gives no reward
NRT supplies nicotine; it doesn't block receptors.
Replaces nicotine and tar but without carbon monoxide
There's no tar in NRT.
Speeds nicotine metabolism to shorten withdrawal
It replaces nicotine to ease withdrawal.
items.sewhy: Nicotine stimulates nicotinic receptors: patches irritate skin, oral forms cause nausea and hiccups, and overnight patches disturb sleep.

ci.c: Recent MI or stroke, unstable arrhythmia
ci.why: Nicotine raises HR and BP, but smoking is worse: specialist advice
x: Nicotine causes coronary thrombosis; never use after MI
Smoking is worse than NRT; get specialist advice rather than avoiding it.
Nicotine lowers BP dangerously; halve the dose
It raises heart rate and BP.
Patches interact with antiplatelets: stop aspirin
No interaction; nicotine raises HR and BP, but smoking is worse.
